Time-of-use electricity: compare the energy you can shift and the whole monthly bill

Hold total monthly kWh constant while moving part of on-peak use, then separate energy-charge savings, unchanged fees and the percentage change in a simplified bill.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 5 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Move a selected share of on-peak energy while keeping total kWh fixed

Interactive planning lab

Simplified monthly bill before the shift$118
Simplified monthly bill after the shift$109.6
Monthly saving from timing alone; negative means higher cost$8.4

Original hypothetical three-period monthly energy bill, not an Ontario tariff, utility quote or full actual bill estimate. Prices are entered in cents per kWh and divided by 100 for CAD charges. The selected fraction of original on-peak consumption moves to off-peak, with no change in total energy, mid-peak use or the entered fixed amount. 70 kWh move within a total of 700 kWh. The consumption-weighted energy price changes from 14.00 to 12.80 cents/kWh. The simplified whole bill falls by 7.12%. The tool does not determine whether the assumed energy can actually be shifted. The fixed amount represents only charges chosen to remain unchanged; it does not assert that every delivery or non-energy charge on a real bill is fixed. Variable delivery charges, losses, demand charges, tiers, taxes, rebates, seasonal price schedules, equipment costs and changes in efficiency are excluded. The period labels do not enforce a price hierarchy: a higher entered off-peak rate can make the shift more expensive.

The central idea

A cheaper price applies only to the energy moved into that period. Use consumption weights and keep unchanged charges separate before estimating the whole-bill saving.

01

Identify which part of the bill a timing change can affect

A lower off-peak energy price can be useful, but it does not apply automatically to every kilowatt-hour or every charge on the monthly bill. The planning calculation begins with the amount of energy that can move and the charges that remain unchanged.

The Ontario Energy Board’s bill explanation distinguishes electricity charges that depend on time of use from other bill components. It also explains that some delivery charges are fixed while others vary. That supports reading the parts of the bill separately, rather than treating the entire invoice as one energy price.

This tool uses a simplified, original three-period bill: hypothetical energy prices of 20 cents/kWh on-peak, 12 cents mid-peak and 8 cents off-peak, plus CAD 20 assumed unchanged each month. These are not current Ontario prices or a utility quote. Other variable delivery charges, losses, demand charges, taxes, tiers and rebates are outside the calculation.

02

Weight the energy prices by actual use instead of averaging the rate labels

The starting allocation is 280 kWh on-peak, 210 kWh mid-peak and 210 kWh off-peak, totalling 700 kWh. The energy costs are CAD 56, CAD 25.20 and CAD 16.80, respectively. Adding them gives a variable energy charge of CAD 98.

The consumption-weighted energy price is CAD 98 ÷ 700 kWh, or 14 cents/kWh. That differs from the unweighted average of the three rate labels: (20 + 12 + 8) ÷ 3, or about 13.33 cents. The household has not used equal quantities in each period, so equal weighting answers a different question.

Adding the unchanged CAD 20 produces the simplified baseline bill of CAD 118. The fixed amount has a separate role; it is not another energy rate applied to the 700 kWh. Likewise, this energy-only weighted rate is not a complete all-in rate for a real utility bill.

03

A quarter of on-peak use is not a quarter of total use

The default shift is 25% of the original on-peak 280 kWh. That moves 70 kWh to off-peak. Since the entire month contains 700 kWh, the shifted amount is only 10% of total consumption.

After the shift, on-peak and mid-peak use are both 210 kWh, while off-peak use rises to 280 kWh. Total energy remains 700 kWh. The first chart makes that conservation visible: the amount removed from one period appears in the other rather than disappearing from the bill.

This is a timing example, not an energy-efficiency improvement. It assumes that moving the selected use does not increase other consumption, change the service provided or require equipment spending. The tool cannot establish whether a particular household can actually move that fraction of its use.

04

Subtract the new charge from the charge avoided

The shifted 70 kWh would cost 70 × CAD 0.20 = CAD 14 on-peak. In the off-peak period it costs 70 × CAD 0.08 = CAD 5.60. The saving is therefore CAD 8.40 per modeled month, which is also 70 kWh × the CAD 0.12 price difference.

The waterfall keeps both sides of that change visible. Avoiding the original charge is only the first step; the energy still needs to be paid for in the new period. The unchanged charges and all energy that did not move cancel when comparing the two allocations.

The after-shift energy charge is CAD 89.60. With the unchanged CAD 20, the simplified bill becomes CAD 109.60. No payment or rebate of CAD 8.40 is assumed; that amount is cash spending avoided relative to the original allocation.

05

Keep the denominator beside each percentage

The off-peak unit price is 60% below the on-peak price in this authored example: (20 − 8) ÷ 20. That comparison applies to the price of the 70 kWh moved, not to all 700 kWh or the complete bill.

The variable energy charge falls by CAD 8.40 ÷ CAD 98, or about 8.57%. The simplified whole bill falls by CAD 8.40 ÷ CAD 118, or about 7.12%. The consumption-weighted energy price changes from 14.0 to 12.8 cents/kWh, while total use stays fixed.

All three percentages can be correct at once because their denominators differ. Describing the 60% unit-price reduction as a 60% bill saving would apply a limited change to a much larger base.

Increase the unchanged monthly amount from CAD 20 to CAD 60 and the dollar saving remains CAD 8.40. The baseline bill becomes CAD 158, so its percentage reduction is about 5.32%. An unchanged charge affects the share of the bill saved even though it does not alter the energy-cost difference.

06

Test the achievable shift and price spread separately

The final chart varies the fraction of original on-peak use moved from zero to 100%, keeping the entered quantities, rates and unchanged charge otherwise fixed. The original bill remains a reference line. At zero shift the two bills coincide; with no on-peak use, every shift setting has the same result.

The period names alone do not enforce a lower price in the arithmetic. If the entered off-peak rate exceeds the on-peak rate, moving energy raises the modeled bill and the saving metric becomes negative. If the two rates match, timing alone produces no energy saving.

Changing only the selected shift updates the headline result and allocation bars while leaving the full-range comparison curve in place. The curve does not assign a likelihood to any amount of shifted use or establish what a household’s appliances can achieve.

07

Use the actual bill before putting a saving into the household plan

  1. Record the relevant energy quantities and price periods from the bill.
  2. Identify a feasible amount of use to move rather than assuming every kWh can shift.
  3. Separate unchanged charges from all other charges that vary.
  4. Compare the complete applicable tariff and any switching or equipment costs.
  5. Review different seasons before projecting an annual saving.

Twelve identical example months would produce CAD 100.80 of timing savings. That is a repeated-case calculation, not an annual forecast: usage, rates, period definitions and the amount that can move may differ through the year.

The illustration does not compare actual electricity plans or determine eligibility for them. It explains how a selected timing change passes through an intentionally simple bill. The related utility-payment and upgrade guides address different questions about payment schedules and changes in energy use.
